section.title: A Time for Everything
section.sectionRationale: After chasing pleasure, work, and wisdom and finding them all vapor, the Teacher lifts his eyes to the rhythm of the seasons. Everything has its appointed time, set by a God who works beyond our sight. The chapter moves from the famous poem of the times, through the confession that God has made everything beautiful in its time and set eternity in the human heart, to the sobering truth that man and beast share one breath and return to one dust. The answer under the sun is small but real: fear God, and receive food, work, and joy from His hand.
section.thesis: God has fixed a time for everything and does all things well, yet He hides the whole from us and sets eternity in our hearts, so that we cannot master life but are driven to fear Him and to receive daily bread, work, and joy as His gift.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the poem of the times, a season for every purpose under heaven; the burden and the gift, God's work endures and He has set eternity in the heart; and from dust to dust, where judgment, death, and the shared breath of man and beast press the reader back to God.

verses.text: To everything there is a {{zeman|season}}, and a {{eth|time}} for every purpose under heaven:
a time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to uproot,
a time to kill and a time to heal, a time to break down and a time to build,
a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance,
a time to cast away stones and a time to gather stones together, a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing,
a time to search and a time to count as lost, a time to keep and a time to discard,
a time to tear and a time to mend, a time to be silent and a time to speak,
a time to love and a time to hate, a time for war and a time for peace.
What does the worker gain from his toil?
I have seen the burden that God has laid upon the sons of men to occupy them.
He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set {{olam|eternity}} in the hearts of men, yet they cannot fathom the work that God has done from beginning to end.
I know that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice and do good while they live,
and also that every man should eat and drink and find satisfaction in all his labor, this is the gift of God.
I know that everything God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it or taken from it. God does it so that they should fear Him.
What exists has already been, and what will be has already been, for God will call to account what has passed.

units.label: From dust to dust
units.note: one breath for man and beast

verses.text: Furthermore, I saw under the sun that in the place of judgment there is wickedness, and in the place of righteousness there is wickedness.
I said in my heart, “God will judge the righteous and the wicked, since there is a time for every activity and every deed.”
I said to myself, “As for the sons of men, God tests them so that they may see for themselves that they are but beasts.”

For the fates of both men and beasts are the same: As one dies, so dies the other, they all have the same {{ruach|breath}}. Man has no advantage over the animals, since everything is {{hevel|futile}}.
All go to one place; all come from dust, and all return to dust.
Who knows if the {{ruach|spirit}} of man rises upward and the spirit of the animal descends into the earth?
I have seen that there is nothing better for a man than to enjoy his work, because that is his lot. For who can bring him to see what will come after him?

zeman.gloss: An appointed season or fixed time. Paired here with eth, it opens the poem: every purpose under heaven has a season already set by God, not left to chance or to human control.

eth.gloss: A time, an occasion, the right moment. It drums through the poem twenty eight times, a time to be born, a time to die, insisting that the moments of a life fall within times that God has appointed.

olam.gloss: Eternity, the far distance of time past and future, the everlasting. God has set olam in the human heart: a sense of forever, a longing that outruns this life, which nothing under the sun can satisfy.

ruach.gloss: Breath, wind, or spirit. Man and beast share one ruach and return to dust; yet the same word opens the question of whether the spirit of man rises upward, a hope the whole canon answers in the resurrection.

hevel.gloss: Vapor, breath, mist. The keyword of the book, rendered futile, meaningless, or fleeting. It names how life under the sun slips through the fingers like breath on a cold morning, here because man, like the beast, dies and returns to dust.

basic.context: Having tried pleasure, work, and wisdom and found them all like vapor, the Teacher steps back to look at the shape of time itself. The famous poem in verses 1 to 8 says that everything, birth and death, weeping and laughing, war and peace, has its appointed season. Then he asks the honest question: if God has set all these times, what do we actually gain by our toil? His answer is humbling. God has made everything beautiful in its time and has put a sense of eternity in our hearts, yet He does not let us see the whole picture. So the best thing is to fear God and receive food, work, and joy as gifts from His hand, even though man and beast alike return to the dust.
basic.hermeneutics: The poem is not fatalism, as if we were trapped in a machine. It is a wisdom picture of a world ordered by a sovereign God, meant to teach humility and trust rather than despair. The key question is what verse 11 means by eternity in the heart: God has planted in us a longing for what is forever, which is why nothing temporary ever fully satisfies. The darkness of verses 18 to 21, that we share one breath with the animals and go to the same dust, is real and is meant to drive us to God, not to numb us.
basic.originalLanguages: The poem hammers one word, eth, time, and pairs it with zeman, season: God has fixed the times. In verse 11 God sets olam, eternity, in the heart, a longing for forever that this world cannot fill. In verses 19 and 21 the word ruach, breath or spirit, links man and beast, both die and return to dust, yet ruach also opens the question of whether the spirit of man rises upward. And the summary word of the book, hevel, vapor, names how fleeting all of this is under the sun.
basic.typology: The eternity God sets in the heart is a God shaped ache that only the eternal Son can fill. The time to be born and a time to die finds its answer in the One who was born to die and then rose, breaking the grip of the dust. The judgment the Teacher expects, God will judge the righteous and the wicked, points to the day when Christ will judge the living and the dead.
basic.christ: The longing for eternity that nothing under the sun can satisfy is met in Jesus, who offers eternal life. The dust to dust verdict of verse 20 is exactly what Christ entered and overturned: He was made subject to futility, died, and rose, so that the spirit of man rising upward is no longer only a question but a hope secured. The One who makes everything beautiful in its time made the fullness of time arrive in Christ.
basic.god: God is sovereign over every season; He makes everything beautiful in its time, and what He does endures forever. He is generous, giving food, drink, work, and joy as gifts. He is also hidden, refusing to let us fathom His work from beginning to end, so that we would fear Him rather than master Him. And He is the just Judge who will call every deed to account.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 8 says creation was subjected to futility in hope, and will be set free. Psalm 90 pleads teach us to number our days. Acts 17 says God has determined appointed times. John 3 and 17 answer the ache for eternity with eternal life in Christ.
basic.oneStory: This is the honest verdict of life under the sun: God orders every season, but we cannot see the whole, and we return to the dust like the beasts. The ache for eternity He plants in us is answered only outside the sun, in the God who made time and then entered it in Christ to conquer death, so that the longing for forever finds its home.

context.literary:
The chapter splits cleanly into a poem and a series of reflections on it. Verses 1 to 8 are the famous poem. Verse 1 states the thesis, and verses 2 to 8 give fourteen pairs of opposites, twenty-eight 'times' in all, spread across seven verses. The numbers are not accidental: seven and its double give the sense of a complete round. The poem opens with birth and death, the two bookends of a life, and closes with love and hate, war and peace, the two bookends of human society. Between them it runs through farming, healing, building, grief, joy, intimacy, loss, speech and silence.

The pairs are what scholars call merisms: naming two extremes to include everything between them. 'Born and die' means the whole span of life. The pairs are also not all pleasant. A time to kill, to tear, to hate and to make war stand beside planting and mending. The poem is a catalogue of what life actually contains, not a list of approved behaviors.

Verse 9 then drops the question that shapes everything after: what does the worker gain from his toil? The poem does not itself answer it. Verses 10 to 15 reflect on God's work: the burden, the beauty, the eternity set in the heart, the permanence of what God does. Verses 16 to 22 move to a darker panel, injustice in the courts, the shared fate of humans and animals, and the unknowable destination of the spirit.

The chapter's final sentence comes back to the refrain of the previous chapter: nothing is better than to enjoy one's work, 'because that is his lot.' The structure is therefore a frame: the seasons of verses 1 to 8, then two reflections that each end in a call to enjoy what God has given, verses 12 to 13 and verse 22. Between those calls the Teacher faces the two biggest limits on human knowledge, that we cannot see the whole of God's work, verse 11, and that we cannot see past death, verse 21.
context.historical:
Israel lived by a calendar. Farming had its seasons of sowing and harvest, Leviticus 23 set out the appointed feasts, and Deuteronomy 16 ordered the year around pilgrimage. Birth, marriage and death had their rites. Hearing a poem about 'times' would have called to mind a life lived in rhythm, with festivals and fasts, mourning and dancing, set out for the community.

Some of the pairs have concrete background. 'Cast away stones and gather stones together,' verse 5, may refer to the work of clearing a field or, in the language of 2 Kings 3:19 and 3:25, to ruining a field by throwing stones on it, so that the same act can mean damage or labor. Ancient readers also knew the stones of building and the scattered stones of a ruined city. 'A time to tear and a time to mend,' verse 7, fits the custom of tearing garments in grief, as Jacob did when he thought Joseph was dead, Genesis 37:34, and the later mending when the mourning was done. 'A time for war and a time for peace' sat in the lap of a small nation between great powers.

Other ancient peoples also reflected on fate and the rhythm of the world. Ecclesiastes shares the awareness of rhythm but gives it a different source. The times are given by a personal God, and the text says that the person who knows this can fear Him, verse 14.

The courtroom scene of verse 16 also has a setting. The 'place of judgment' was the city gate, where elders heard cases, as in Ruth 4:1-2 and Amos 5:12. The Law told judges to hear impartially, Deuteronomy 16:18-20, and the prophets denounced judges who took bribes. Verse 16 is a lament that the very places set up for justice are infected, and verse 17 is the Teacher's assurance that there is a higher court.
context.canonical:
The poem has a long afterlife. Behind it stands the creation account in which God sets lights in the sky 'for seasons, days and years,' Genesis 1:14, and calls everything good, Genesis 1:31. The Teacher's 'He has made everything beautiful in its time' reads that verdict through the lens of time. The curse of Genesis 3:19 stands behind the last verses: 'all come from dust, and all return to dust' is the sentence repeated, and Genesis 2:7 is the origin of the 'breath' of verse 19.

The Psalms pray the same convictions. 'My times are in Your hands,' Psalm 31:15. 'So teach us to number our days,' Psalm 90:12, after the confession that God returns man to dust. Psalm 104:29-30 says that when God takes away the breath of creatures they die and return to dust, and when He sends His Spirit they are created. Psalm 146:3-4 tells readers not to trust princes, because when the spirit departs a man returns to the ground and his plans perish.

Within the book the poem is picked up in 7:14, where prosperity and adversity both come from God, 8:5-6, where there is a time and a way for every matter, and in the closing poem on old age and death, 12:1-7, whose last verse answers 3:21: 'the spirit returns to God who gave it.'

The New Testament speaks of time in the same two Greek words the Septuagint uses here, kairos and chronos. Jesus begins His ministry with 'the time is fulfilled,' Mark 1:15, and Paul says God sent His Son 'when the time had fully come,' Galatians 4:4. In Acts, Jesus tells the disciples it is not for them to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed, Acts 1:7, and Paul says God 'determined their appointed times' for the nations, Acts 17:26. Paul echoes the Teacher's word for futility and sets creation's groaning in hope, Romans 8:20-23, and 1 Corinthians 15:54 announces that death has been swallowed up in victory.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The Teacher wants his hearers to accept that life is given to them in seasons they do not control, and that this is not a cause for despair. People who try to hold every season at once, or who believe they can mandate the outcome of each, will be broken. The poem invites a posture of discernment: to recognize which time one is in and to act accordingly, to weep when it is time to weep and to laugh when it is time to laugh.

Yet he does not let the poem finish the matter. The gap between the beauty of God's ordering and our limited sight, verse 11, is an honest word to people who want to see the whole. He wants them to live with the question, not to be silenced by it. God's work is whole, and ours is a piece.

The second half of the chapter pushes the hearers into the hard cases: injustice, death, the animal-like end of the body. He means them to learn humility, since neither human power nor human wisdom can fix those things. And three times he returns to the same counsel: enjoy what God gives you, because that is the portion you can reach. He wants his hearers to fear God, verse 14, to expect judgment, verse 17, and to rejoice in the work in front of them, verse 22.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The poem describes the range of human experience; it does not approve every item. A time to kill and to hate are not commands to do so, and nothing in the poem says that any moment justifies murder or malice. The same Law that notes war also forbids murder, Exodus 20:13, and the same Bible calls believers to love enemies, Matthew 5:44. The poem reports that such things happen in the world and asks hearers to recognize the moment they are in, not to excuse their sins.

Nor is the poem a fatalistic law of nature, as if nothing can be done. The Teacher uses it to cut down illusions of control, not to cancel responsibility. The same book tells people to act wisely, to sow in the morning and evening, 11:6, and to work with all their might, 9:10.

What it does prescribe is wise timing. Proverbs 15:23 praises the timely word, and the Teacher makes the same point: there is a time to speak and a time to be silent. A believer may take the chapter as permission to grieve at funerals and to dance at weddings, and as a warning against forcing either into the wrong hour. The call at the end, to enjoy one's work, is a summary of what to do inside the limits of verse 11.

debates.question: What does it mean that God has set 'eternity' in human hearts, verse 11?

views.label: A sense of the timeless
views.case: The BSB reads olam as eternity: God has given humans a longing for something beyond the present moment, which makes it impossible for any season to satisfy fully. This fits the lines before, where beauty is bound to time, and after, where people cannot fathom God's whole work. It also resonates with the ache for the unseen that Paul describes in 2 Corinthians 4:18.

views.label: The world or the whole course of time
views.case: Older English versions, such as the King James, read 'the world in their heart,' taking the word as the world or the long expanse of time, so that people have an awareness of the whole but cannot trace its design.

views.label: A tension rather than a gift
views.case: Some commentators propose that the word should be read in another form to mean something like ignorance or concealment, so that the verse says God put darkness in the heart. Most translations keep the more natural 'eternity' or 'world,' but the proposal shows how disputed the word is.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that human beings sense more than they can grasp. The most natural reading pairs a sense of the timeless with an inability to see the end from the beginning, and that is exactly the condition that makes trust in God, rather than control, the only workable response.

debates.question: Does the Teacher doubt life after death in verses 19 to 21?

views.label: Real agnosticism
views.case: The opening claim that humans have no advantage over animals, and the question 'Who knows?', suggest a writer who does not know whether the spirit survives. Some read the whole book as honest uncertainty before the fuller revelation of the New Testament.

views.label: A rhetorical question with an answer elsewhere
views.case: The question, 'who knows if the spirit of man rises upward,' sits beside 12:7, 'the spirit returns to God who gave it.' The Teacher draws the picture of the world as seen from below, and the book's end shows the conviction that God receives the spirit.

views.label: A deliberate limit of 'under the sun'
views.case: Because the refrain frames everything from the observer's side of the grave, the Teacher is describing what observation can and cannot prove. He is correcting those who assume they know the answer, not denying it.

debates.bearing: The text does not settle the matter in this chapter, and the honest reader should say so. The second and third views are strengthened by 12:7 and 12:14, and the New Testament supplies the proof the Teacher lacks, in the resurrection of Christ, Acts 17:31.

debates.question: What does the Teacher mean that 'there is a time' for every activity: is it fate or wise timing?

views.label: Fixed determinism
views.case: Verse 1 speaks of an appointed time, and verse 14 says what God does endures and nothing can be added to it or taken away. On this reading the poem pictures a set order that humans can only receive.

views.label: Appropriate timing within a wise life
views.case: The language of 'time' is about fitness: the right moment for the right act. This matches wisdom literature, where Proverbs 15:23 praises the apt word, and verse 11 says all is beautiful 'in its time,' not 'in every time.'

debates.bearing: The chapter holds both: God's order is sure, and humans are called to discern. Nothing in the text turns that into passivity, since verse 12 tells people to rejoice and do good while they live.

study.originalLanguages:
The first verse uses two words for time, zeman and eth, and the second of them runs through the poem twenty-eight times. The word for 'purpose' in verse 1 is chephets, a word for what one delights in or desires. It is used of God's pleasure too: God 'takes no pleasure,' ein chephets, in fools, 5:4, and the same word returns for 'activity' in 3:17. Every matter under heaven has its season, and the word suggests that each matter is something someone wants and cares about, not just a mechanical event. The Septuagint renders the two time words as chronos and kairos, the same two Greek words the New Testament uses in Galatians 4:4 and Mark 1:15.

In verse 2 the first pair is laledet, literally 'to bear' or 'to give birth,' and lamut, 'to die.' The infinitive can be read either way, and both fit: a time to be born, a time to bear. Whichever way it is taken, the poem begins at the gate of life and ends in war and peace, the broadest frame it can draw.

The 'burden' of verse 10 is 'inyan, a word for occupation or business that returns from 1:13, where God gave the same burden to occupy the sons of men. The root idea is being kept busy. What the BSB calls a burden is also what keeps humans from idleness, and the Teacher uses the same word in both places, calling it ra, evil or heavy, in 1:13 and leaving it unqualified here.

In verse 11 the word 'beautiful' is yapheh, the word for the beauty of a woman or a city, the aesthetic judgment that echoes Genesis 1:31, 'very good.' God has made everything yapheh in its eth. The 'eternity' is olam, and the line 'from beginning to end,' me-rosh ve-ad sof, sets the boundaries of what humans cannot fathom. The heart can sense the whole without seeing its edges.

Verse 12's phrase 'to rejoice and do good' is ambiguous in the Hebrew. 'To do good,' la-asot tov, can mean to act well morally or to fare well, to have a good life. Ancient and modern translators differ, and the sense of both is likely in view.

Verse 15 says God 'will call to account what has passed.' The Hebrew has the verb baqash, to seek, with a form of the verb radaf, to pursue, so the line is literally close to 'God seeks what is pursued.' Translators differ on whether it means God requires an account for the past, recovers what is chased away, or repeats the pattern of events. The BSB takes the first sense.

In verses 18 to 21 the animals are behemah, the ordinary word for beasts and cattle, and the shared lot is miqreh, 'fate,' used three times in verse 19. The word for breath is ruach, and the question of verse 21, 'who knows,' mi yodea, is the same rhetorical question the book uses elsewhere to mark the limits of human knowledge. Verse 20 echoes Genesis 3:19 closely, the earth to which all return and the dust from which all come, and Ecclesiastes 12:7 uses the verb 'return' for both the dust and the spirit, giving each its own destination.

typology.type: The appointed time that arrives in Christ, Ecclesiastes 3:1
typology.fulfillment: Ecclesiastes says there is an appointed time for every purpose, and the Gospels show the Son living by a divine timetable. At Cana He says, 'My hour has not yet come,' John 2:4, and He tells His brothers, 'My time has not yet come,' John 7:6. On the night of His arrest, 'the hour has come,' Mark 14:41, and John 17:1 opens His prayer with the same words. Paul says God sent His Son 'when the time had fully come,' Galatians 4:4. The pattern of seasons becomes the pattern of a history directed toward its center. The correspondence is not total, since Ecclesiastes' times recur and Christ's hour happens once.

typology.type: Dust and the breath of life, Ecclesiastes 3:19-21
typology.fulfillment: The Teacher sees humans as creatures of dust who return to dust, under the sentence of Genesis 3:19. Paul sets the first man, 'of the dust of the earth,' beside the second man 'from heaven,' 1 Corinthians 15:47. The Teacher's question, 'who knows if the spirit of man rises upward,' meets its answer in the One who commended His spirit to the Father and rose, Luke 23:46 and Acts 17:31. Believers who bore the likeness of the earthly man will bear the likeness of the heavenly man, 1 Corinthians 15:49. The type falls short in that the Teacher states the shared fate; Christ alone breaks it and offers a different end.

typology.type: A time to weep and a time to laugh, Ecclesiastes 3:4
typology.fulfillment: The pair of weeping and laughing finds an echo in Jesus. He wept at the tomb of Lazarus, John 11:35, and over Jerusalem, Luke 19:41, entering the grief the Teacher records. Yet He also promises, 'Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh,' Luke 6:21. The seasons become a direction: the weeping is real, and it is headed toward a day when God wipes away every tear, Revelation 21:4. The correspondence falls short of the Teacher's poem in one respect, since there the seasons simply alternate, while Christ's promise is that the laughter will not be followed by a new mourning.

study.christ:
The poem of the seasons leads to Christ by pointing to a Lord of time. The Teacher knows that God has fixed a time for every matter, and the Gospels show the Son carrying out that order. Jesus does not drift through events. He keeps an appointment: His hour is held back at Cana and the feast in John 2 and 7, and then it arrives. When it does, He says, 'Father, the hour has come,' John 17:1. Paul's phrase 'at just the right time, while we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly,' Romans 5:6, shows why the Teacher's question about profit under the sun is not left hanging. The deepest 'time' of all is the cross, and it was appointed.

It leads to Christ by the puzzle of the shared end. The Teacher sees one place for all, and asks who knows whether the spirit rises. In Christ the question gets an answer from outside the sun's circuit. He took on our flesh and blood and, by His death, destroyed him who holds the power of death, Hebrews 2:14-15. His resurrection is the firstfruits of a harvest, 1 Corinthians 15:20-23, and God has 'given proof of this to everyone by raising Him from the dead,' Acts 17:31. The earthly man returned to dust. The heavenly man came out of the grave and will bring those who are His, 1 Corinthians 15:47-49.

It leads to Christ by the injustice of verse 16. The Teacher sees wickedness in the very seat of judgment and holds on to the assurance that God will judge. The New Testament says the judge is the Man God appointed, Acts 17:31, and shows Him taking the place of the condemned. The One who was wrongly judged by a corrupt court is the One who will judge with justice. A man who suffered the failure of human courts is the answer to the question of whether justice will come.

It leads to Christ by the burden of grief. Jesus does not stand above the poem; He enters it. He weeps, John 11:35, and Hebrews 4:15 says He sympathizes with our weaknesses. He rejoices, and He tells His disciples that their grief will turn to joy, John 16:20. The warning is not to treat every pair in the poem as a hidden allegory. The better reading is that Christ gathers the whole range of human seasons into His own life, bears the worst of them, and promises an eternal season in which the tears are wiped away.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who orders time without being bound by it. He appoints a season for every matter, makes everything beautiful in its time, and does works that endure, to which nothing can be added and from which nothing can be taken away, verse 14. Psalm 90:2 says He is God 'from everlasting to everlasting,' and Psalm 31:15 says our times are in His hands. The Teacher's instinct is that human life is held inside a larger life.

The chapter also shows a God who hides some of His work. Humans have a sense of the whole but cannot trace it from start to finish, verse 11. Isaiah 55:8-9 and Romans 11:33 say the same: His ways are higher and His judgments unsearchable. This is not a God who is cruel or arbitrary; it is a God who is greater than the creature's mind. The purpose of that hiddenness is given in verse 14: He does it so that people should fear Him. Reverence is the right response to a God who cannot be audited.

The chapter holds God's goodness and His sovereignty together with the experience of evil. He made everything beautiful, and yet there is wickedness in the place of justice. The Teacher does not blame God, and he does not deny the wickedness. He says God will judge both the righteous and the wicked, verse 17, and that time and judgment belong to Him. Acts 17:31 says the day is set.

The chapter shows God as a giver of gifts in the middle of a hard world: rejoicing, doing good, eating and drinking and finding satisfaction in toil are 'the gift of God,' verse 13. God is not stingy, and He does not cancel joy because the world is fallen.

For worship, the chapter teaches a kind of humility that is also freedom. A person who knows God holds all the times can stop pretending to hold them. Prayer becomes the act of handing over what we cannot see, and thanks becomes the act of receiving what is given today. Psalm 90:12 asks God to teach us to number our days so that we may gain a heart of wisdom, which is the lesson of this chapter turned into prayer.

crossReferences.note: God looked at all He had made and called it very good. The Teacher's 'He has made everything beautiful in its time' reads that verdict in the key of time: creation's goodness is real, but it unfolds in seasons that people do not control.

The sentence of dust is the background of verse 20: 'all come from dust, and all return to dust.' The Teacher is not inventing a gloomy view; he is naming the consequence that the fall brought on every creature.
A believer in trouble prays, 'My times are in Your hands.' It is the devout form of verse 1: the seasons that frustrate human control are safe because they are held by God.
After confessing that God returns man to dust, Moses asks God to teach us to number our days. It is the prayer that the Teacher's observations produce, turning awareness of mortality into wisdom.

The closing poem on death says the dust returns to the ground and the spirit returns to God who gave it. It stands as a firm reply to the question of 3:21, showing that the book does not end where this chapter pauses.

Paul tells the Athenians that God determined the appointed times of the nations and the boundaries of their lands. The appointment of times is not a private Hebrew idea but a claim about all human history.
God sent His Son when the time had fully come. The Teacher's poem of fixed seasons is carried to its center: history has an hour that was waiting for a person.
Jesus opens His ministry with 'The time is fulfilled.' The Greek word is kairos, the same word the Septuagint uses for 'time' in the poem, and it marks a decisive season rather than a recurring one.

Creation groans like a woman in labor, and believers groan as they wait for the redemption of their bodies. It gives the burden of verse 10 and the futility of verse 19 a direction: they are labor pains, not a dead end.
Man is appointed to die once and afterward to face judgment. It joins the Teacher's two certainties, the shared death of verse 20 and the coming judgment of verse 17, into one sentence.
Paul fixes his eyes on the unseen and eternal, because what is seen is temporary. It reads the eternity set in the heart as a pull toward what cannot be seen from within the seasons.
God will wipe away every tear, and there will be no more death or mourning. The weeping and mourning of verse 4 and the death of verse 2 are given an end, and the former things pass away.

study.oneStory:
Genesis opens with time: evening and morning, the lights set for seasons, a week that ends in rest. Ecclesiastes 3 takes that ordered, good creation and walks it through the fall, where the same order carries birth and death, building and tearing down. The poem shows a world that is still God's, still beautiful in its time, and still under the shadow of Genesis 3:19.

What the passage answers from before is the question of why a good world holds so much grief. The Bible's answer is not that the seasons are bad but that human beings fell out of right relationship with the Giver of the seasons, so that every season is now touched by loss. What the passage sets up is the need for someone who can stand outside the cycle. The Teacher cannot see from beginning to end, and he knows it. The story needs a person who can.

That person comes 'when the time had fully come,' Galatians 4:4. Ephesians 1:9-10 says God purposed in Christ a plan for the fullness of time, to bring all things in heaven and on earth together. The Lord of the hours enters the hours, weeps at a tomb, takes the sentence of the dust, and rises. The Teacher's question about whether the spirit goes up is answered at Easter, and the firstfruits guarantee the harvest, 1 Corinthians 15:20.

The seasons themselves are not abolished at once. The church lives between the first coming and the second, in a time where it still weeps and still laughs, and where it still has to wait for what it cannot see. Romans 8:22-25 describes this as groaning with hope, and Paul asks believers to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep, Romans 12:15, which is the Teacher's poem lived as love.

The story ends where the poem cannot go. Isaiah 25:8 promises that God will swallow up death forever, and Revelation 21:1-5 shows the new heaven and new earth, where God makes His home with His people, wipes every tear, and ends death, mourning, crying and pain. Then the 'former things' pass away, and the times of tearing down and uprooting are over. What God makes beautiful in its time will be beautiful without the shadow, and the eternity set in the heart will find what it was made for.

quiz.q: What is the main point of the poem in 3:1-8?

options.text: God has appointed a season for every purpose, so life's times are under His sovereign ordering.
options.note: The repeated a time to underlines that God, not chance, sets the seasons of life.

options.text: Life is a series of opposite experiences that balance each other out.
options.note: The pattern of opposites is real, but the deeper point is that God appoints each time.

options.text: We are trapped by fate and our efforts change nothing.
options.note: The chapter reads the times as God's wise ordering, not a blind machine.

options.text: We should try to control the timing of everything ourselves.
options.note: The poem teaches the opposite: the times belong to God, not to us.

quiz.q: What does it mean that God has set eternity in the human heart, 3:11?

options.text: God has planted a longing for the everlasting that nothing temporary can satisfy.
options.note: The ache for forever is why life under the sun never fully fills us.

options.text: God has given us a sense of the vast sweep of time we cannot fully grasp.
options.note: A fair reading, and it points the same way, toward trusting the God who sees the whole.

options.text: God has made us able to figure out His plans from beginning to end.
options.note: The verse says the opposite, that we cannot fathom His work.

options.text: God has promised everyone eternal life regardless of anything.
options.note: The verse names a longing, not a blanket promise; that longing is met in Christ.

quiz.q: What does the Teacher commend as the good response within this life?

options.text: To fear God and to receive food, work, and joy as gifts from His hand.
options.note: Verses 12 to 14 and 22 hold together fearing God and enjoying His gifts.

options.text: To eat, drink, and enjoy one's work as a God given lot.
options.note: True, but it leaves out the anchor, the fear of God in verse 14.

options.text: To work harder so that our toil finally pays off.
options.note: The chapter questions what toil gains and points instead to gift and to fearing God.

options.text: To stop caring about anything since all is fleeting.
options.note: The Teacher counsels reverent joy, not numb indifference.

quiz.q: Why does the Teacher dwell on man and beast sharing one breath and one dust, 3:18-21?

options.text: To humble us before death and drive us to fear God rather than trust ourselves.
options.note: The shared dust exposes our frailty and presses us back to God.

options.text: To show that human life is fragile and ends like every other creature's.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but the aim is to humble us toward God, not merely to observe frailty.

options.text: To prove that there is no difference at all between people and animals.
options.note: He raises the question of the spirit rising upward, hinting at a real difference and a hope.

options.text: To teach that death is the final word and nothing lies beyond.
options.note: The canon answers his open question with resurrection hope in Christ.

quiz.q: How does this chapter point forward to Christ?

options.text: The eternity in the heart and the dust of death are answered by Christ, who gives eternal life and conquers the grave.
options.note: The ache for forever and the verdict of dust both find their answer in the risen Christ.

options.text: It shows a longing for something more that only God can satisfy.
options.note: True, and that longing is met specifically in Jesus and His resurrection.

options.text: It promises that hard work will always be rewarded in this life.
options.note: The chapter questions the gain of toil and points beyond the sun for the answer.

options.text: It has nothing to do with Christ or the wider Bible.
options.note: The New Testament takes up its themes of futility, eternity, and judgment in Christ.

questions: The poem says there is a time for everything. What season do you sense you are in right now, and how would it change things to entrust its timing to God?
God has set eternity in your heart, a longing nothing temporary can fill. Where have you been trying to satisfy that ache with things that were only ever passing?
The Teacher commends receiving food, work, and joy as gifts from God's hand. What ordinary gift might you have been treating as an achievement rather than receiving with thanks?
God keeps the whole of His work hidden so that we would fear Him. Where do you need to trade the craving to understand everything for simple trust in Him?
Man and beast share the dust, yet Christ has conquered the grave. How does the resurrection change the way you face your own mortality this week?

translationNotes.note: Season translates zeman, an appointed time, and time translates eth, the fitting moment; together they stress that the occasions of life are set by God, not by chance.
Eternity translates olam, the everlasting or the far reach of time; God sets it in the heart, giving us a longing for forever that this world cannot satisfy.
The same word ruach means both breath and spirit; man and beast share one ruach and return to dust, while verse 21 uses it to raise the hope that the spirit of man rises upward.
Futile translates hevel, literally vapor or breath, the book's keyword for what is fleeting and cannot be grasped, not that life is worthless but that it slips away under the sun.
